newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia fails to reach economic targets--chamber.
newsitem.headline: Serbia fails to reach economic targets--chamber.

text.p: Serbia failed to reach its economic goals in the first six months this year mainly due to lack of capital needed to revive its industries, the Serbian Chamber of Commerce said on Tuesday.
The government targeted stability of prices and currency, a 14 percent production and a 37 percent exports growth, structural changes, privatisation and higher standard of living.
"The only bright thing this year is stability of prices and dinar (currency)," said Milosav Filipovic, a member of the Chamber's managing board.

Retail prices in the first six months rose only three percent on December last year. They were up 1.3 percent in January, 0.6 in February and 0.9 percent in March, 0.1 percent in April and 0.2 percent in May.
Retail prices in June dropped 0.1 percent on May.
The official dinar rate remained fixed at 3.3 dinars for a German mark with a black market rate relatively stable at 3.4 to 3.6 dinars for a mark.
Industrial production growth of 8.1 percent in the January-May period compared with the same span in 1996 was encouraging.
"But more dynamic growth is needed if the set target is to be met," Filipovic said, addressing a board meeting.

According to Jadranka Vale, the head of Serbia's Centre for development, production was stagnating. She predicted it would start to decline in up to three months if economic conditions did not change.
The board saw lack of capital as the main reason for the country's bad economic performance.

Serbia managed to raise 1.568 billion German marks of desperately needed funds through a partial sale of its Telekom Srbija to Italian Stet and Greek OTE, out of which 80 percent was paid immediately to the Serbian Development Fund.
The balance is to be paid in January next year.
Chamber vice-president Momir Pavlicevic said credits given by the Fund for export-oriented production were the last chance for the country's economic revival and must not be squandered.
The Fund said it would secure three-, six- and nine-month credits with an annual interest rate of four percent to boost production and support export industries.
"Funds must be invested in production growth and rises in capacity utilisation. This will also push up exports," Vale said.
Serbia's January-June exports stood at $966.2 million, up 27.2 percent on the same period in 1996. Imports were worth $1.953 billion, up 23.4 percent on the same period last year.
"Foreign trade results improved this year, but volume and structure of trade are still not satisfactory," Filipovic said.
"How can we be happy with a deficit of $987.3 million?"
The trade deficit in the first six months this year increased by $163.9 million, 19.9 percent up on the January-June figure in 1996.

A growing number of insolvent firms with an accumulated internal debt of some 8.5 billion dinars ($1.449 billion), financial non-discipline and high taxes burden an economy that was all but shattered by almost four years of war-related international sanctions.
"The targets are not ambitious. We have enough strength, knowledge and resources to achieve them," Mihajlo Milojevic, president of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce, said.
"We must do even more to reach the 1990 level when our gross domestic product stood at $26 billion and annual per capita income at $2,500," he added.
GDP in Serbia and Montenegro, which make up Yugoslavia, stood at $11.618 billion in 1996. Serbia accounts for 95 percent of that amount. ($ = 1.802 German Marks)
